extracted.intended_audience: authors, volume editors, manuscript editors, and publishers preparing book- or journal-length manuscripts for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for preparing, formatting, cross-checking, and copyediting book- and journal-length manuscripts (including multiauthor volumes and previously published material) to meet publisher requirements and house style.

rubrics_metrics.name: List and outline formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use either tabs or the word processor’s list/outline features to create indents, tabs, and numbers/letters/symbols automatically; convert automatically generated numbering to regular text if necessary for publication compatibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text following a list should get a first-line indent only if it is a new paragraph; if it continues the introductory text, it should start flush left. Automatically generated numbers/letters may need conversion for publisher software (normally the editor’s/publisher’s responsibility). See also cross-references to relevant sections (2.12, 6.127-32).

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes and endnotes format
rubrics_metrics.description: Create notes linked to text using the word processor’s footnote/endnote function to take advantage of automatic renumbering; notes should have same line spacing as manuscript and no extra hard returns between notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes may appear as footnotes or chapter/book endnotes in the manuscript (starting over at 1 for each chapter) unless publisher requests otherwise. Do not mix footnotes and endnotes unless necessary. Avoid appending note references to chapter titles. Notes to tables should be numbered separately. See detailed note form guidance (14.24-60) and citation-management considerations (14.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Glossary and abbreviation list formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Each glossary/abbreviation entry should begin on a new line; capitalize term only if it is capitalized in text; separate term and definition with a period, colon, or em dash (pick one consistently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a glossary, begin the definition with a capital letter; in a list of abbreviations, expanded term should reflect its capitalization in running text. Unless all definitions are incomplete sentences, end glossary entries with a period. Terms consistently italicized in text should be italicized in the glossary; abbreviations of italicized terms should generally be italicized. Use same line spacing as manuscript and avoid multiple columns; entries may be flush-and-hang or first-line indented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography and reference list formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Each bibliography/reference-list entry should begin on a new line and use a hanging indent applied via the word processor’s indentation feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never use the Tab key to indent runover lines. Use the same line spacing as the manuscript. For capitalization, italics, and other bibliographic style matters, follow chapter 14 or the applicable style manual. See citation-management software considerations (14.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract and keyword requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may be required to submit abstracts and keywords for books and individual chapters; abstracts are typically separate-file single paragraphs (book abstract ≤500 words; chapter abstracts shorter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstracts should not include tables, lists, illustrations, or notes; publishers often specify word limits. Book abstracts should summarize main arguments and conclusions; chapter abstracts should overview the chapter. Keywords (usually five to ten terms) accompany abstracts to enhance search visibility; each keyword should be a single word or an accepted short compound (e.g., 'table tennis'). Choose keywords carefully as they feed promotional/descriptive metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting illustrations and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers usually prefer separate files for illustrations and often for tables; indicate approximate placement of separate-file illustrations/tables in the text with callouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captions for illustrations should be furnished in a separate file; any list of illustrations should follow the table of contents. Consult publisher guidance about whether tables created in word processors may remain embedded or should be separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artwork submission and labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply text figures (paintings, maps, photographic prints) in digital format or as scans according to publisher specifications; glossy prints must be clearly labeled without impairing quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers often prefer to do their own scans. Label prints on the back or via self-sticking labels. See further illustration guidance (3.15-20).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations may be numbered consecutively or use double numeration (chapter.figure) in scientific/technical/multiauthor/heavily illustrated books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double numeration simplifies renumbering if figures are added/dropped. Illustrations are numbered separately from tables; plates grouped in galleries are numbered separately from interspersed figures. Even if numbers don't appear in final version, assign working numbers to accompany captions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables may be numbered consecutively throughout the book or use double numeration (chapter.table) for many tables or multiauthor works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double numeration simplifies renumbering. Tables are enumerated separately from illustrations. Very simple tabular material may be presented unnumbered in the run of text and then need not have callouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text references vs placement callouts
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between text references (reader-facing, e.g., 'see table 5') and callouts (placement instructions not appearing in published work, e.g., '<table 5 about here>').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the manuscript, enclose callouts in angle brackets or other delimiters on a separate line following the paragraph where the table/illustration is first referred to, or where the author prefers placement. Tables, graphs, and diagrams require both a text reference and a placement callout unless grouped separately. Illustrations not referred to in text usually still require placement callouts. Unnumbered tables in the text do not require callouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting table source notes and other notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Source notes should appear at the foot of the table before other notes and be preceded by the word 'Source' followed by a colon; other table notes may be preceded by 'Note' followed by a colon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific notes follow general notes; notes to each table must be enumerated separately from notes to the text. See fuller discussion (3.76-80).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-checking manuscript components
rubrics_metrics.description: Before submission, cross-check titles/subtitles against table of contents; subheads against table of contents; illustrations vs captions, text references, and callouts; illustration captions vs list of illustrations; tables vs text references and callouts; table titles vs list of tables; internal cross-references/hyperlinks; URLs and external links; quotations against original sources; notes against their text references; notes against bibliography; parenthetical citations vs reference list; abbreviations vs list of abbreviations; contributor names vs table of contents and contributor list in multiauthor works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A thorough cross-check avoids discrepancies that cause production delays and errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking quotations against original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: All quoted matter should be checked against the original sources for both content and source citations before manuscript submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is crucial because manuscript editors may not have access to all sources. Authors should recheck quotations for accuracy, including punctuation; editors should query apparent transcription errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking URLs and external links
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-check URLs and external links mentioned in the text just before submission; update those that no longer point to the intended source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also ensure source citations that include links are complete per chapter 14 guidelines so readers can find resources with or without the link. See 14.6-18 for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifying cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify all cross-references to chapters, sections, appendixes, or sentences before submission; prefer references to chapter/section numbers rather than page numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overusing 'see chapter X above' or page-number references because pagination will change in publication and e-books lack fixed pages. If page numbers are absolutely necessary, use 'p. 000' placeholder to signal later insertion of final pagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing electronic manuscript files and file structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers may prefer separate electronic files for front matter, chapters, appendixes, etc., named according to parts of the table of contents; authors/editors may also work in a single file for convenience—consult publisher guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations should always be in separate files; tables created in word processors may not need separation. Appropriately named separate files help publishers manage complex projects; some prefer single files for ease of searching and use of outline views.

rubrics_metrics.name: File naming and submission checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: File names should correspond to manuscript parts and include author name and descriptive labels; for many parts, prefix numerals to force alphanumeric ordering (e.g., '01 Jones contents', '03 Jones chap01').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not change or delete file extensions. Separate files for illustration captions might use a distinct prefix (e.g., '00 Jones captions'). Electronic artwork files should be named (e.g., 'Jones fig 1.1'). Include a complete list of all submitted files (including captions and illustrations); if PDFs are required list those too. If a hard copy is required, arrange it in table-of-contents order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript page numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Every page (electronic or hard copy) must be numbered; for multiple-file manuscripts, add descriptive page headers next to page numbers to avoid duplicate numbers across files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Files need not be consecutively numbered across a book if submitted as multiple files; use headers like 'Introduction: 1' etc. Arabic numerals may be used for front matter even if roman numerals apply in final publication; the manuscript editor typically indicates where roman numerals apply. In paper-only manuscripts, inserted pages may be numbered 'a' or 'b' (e.g., 55a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Removing comments and tracked changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Delete all embedded comments, hidden text, and tracked changes ('revision marks') from electronic manuscripts before submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outstanding queries should be addressed in a cover letter. The final manuscript must represent the latest version. Manuscript editors should check for hidden text and revision marks and alert author/publisher about potential problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backing up final manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Save backup copies of each crucial stage and at least a backup of the version sent to the publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain copies in at least two separate locations (e.g., computer hard drive and portable drive or secure file-hosting service).

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume editor responsibilities (multiauthor works)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volume editor must determine responsibilities with contributors/publisher and, after ensuring uniform style, typically: collect manuscripts and illustrations in publisher-acceptable form; secure permissions to reproduce copyrighted material; edit each contribution for sense and check references/documentation for uniformity and send edited manuscripts to contributors for approval before submitting volume; provide list of contributors and biographical notes; supply title page, table of contents, prefatory material; send complete manuscript to publisher ensuring latest versions; adhere to publisher schedule and manage contributors' deadlines and whereabouts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many of these responsibilities also apply to journal editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional volume editor responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Depending on publisher arrangement, volume editor may: distribute and collect executed publishing agreements from contributors; check edited manuscripts and respond to queries or distribute edited manuscripts for contributors' review and then check; proofread final version or delegate proofreading and check corrections; prepare index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are conditional on the arrangement with the publisher and should be clarified beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing previously published material (compilation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If compiler retypes or OCRs original sources, incorporate text into a manuscript that follows formatting requirements and proofread word-for-word against originals before submission; publishers may request copies of originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If original material is paper-only, ensure legibility; prefer single-sided legible photocopies or scans to pages from original source. For corrections to paper originals, write in margins if space is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible changes to previously published material
rubrics_metrics.description: Compilers may renumber notes, delete cross-references no longer relevant, and silently correct obvious typographical and inadvertent grammatical slips without editorial comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If wholesale changes are made (spelling, capitalization, notes style), the compiler should note such changes in a preface or elsewhere. Special rules apply for deletions indicated by ellipsis points (see 13.50-58).

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes/endnotes handling in reprinted material
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes appearing as such in originals may be presented as footnotes or endnotes in the reprint; if adding compiler/volume-editor notes along with original notes, intermix them but distinguish new notes from originals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If original material is paper-only, consider producing a separate electronic document for notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source notes for reprinted selections
rubrics_metrics.description: Each selection of previously published material should be accompanied by a headnote or an unnumbered footnote on the first page naming the source, copyright owner if in copyright, and original title if changed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple versions exist, the source note must state which version is being reprinted; a full publishing history is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducing previously published illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compilers should consult publishers on how to obtain illustrations in acceptable print-ready formats; photocopies of illustrations are not acceptable for reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procure glossy prints or original publisher scans; if unavailable, it may be possible to reproduce an illustration from the original publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of manuscript editing and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscript editing (copyediting/line editing) requires attention to every word and punctuation mark, knowledge of the style to be followed, and the ability to make defensible decisions; it may include mechanical editing and substantive editing and is distinct from developmental editing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanical editing applies house/style rules consistently; substantive editing deals with organization and presentation and generally requires agreement between publisher and editor before substantial changes, except that journal editors on tight schedules may perform substantive editing without prior consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical editing standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply a particular style consistently across text, documentation, tables, and illustrations—covering capitalization, spelling, hyphenation, abbreviations, punctuation (ellipsis, parentheses, quotation marks), and number treatment; attend to grammar, syntax, and usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style manual rules may be supplemented by publisher’s house style or discipline-specific style. Works in a series or multivolume should follow one consistent style. The style and any agreed deviations must be determined before editing begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive editing principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive editing addresses organization and presentation, rewriting to improve style or eliminate ambiguity, reorganizing or tightening disorganized sections, and adjusting or recasting tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not undertake substantive editing without agreement between publisher and editor for book-length works; authors should be consulted and may be asked to approve a sample. Journal manuscript editors may need to do substantive editing under schedule constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial discretion and respect for author voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a light editorial hand: recognize and not tamper with unusual figures of speech or idiomatic usage; know when to change and when to suggest, and respect the author’s own style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should know and follow any publisher policies essential to the house (e.g., bias-free language). For communicating with authors and querying, see specified sections (2.68-72).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating editing time
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate editing time realistically, typically based on word count rather than page count; consider complexities of text, documentation, tables, illustrations, electronic formatting, and the publication schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a 100,000-word book edited by an experienced editor might take 75–100 hours before sending to author plus 10–20 hours after author review; if in doubt, edit a small sample to base the estimate on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of manuscript editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors usually work through a manuscript three times—initial editing (longest), a second pass to review/refine/correct, and a third pass after the author’s review; electronic manuscripts may require an initial systematic cleanup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by surveying the whole document to assess scope, identify matters needing clarification, and reduce surprises. Elements (notes, bibliography, tables, figures) may be edited separately or with the text, but all elements must be cross-checked for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference works and dictionary choice
rubrics_metrics.description: A good dictionary and reference works for names, places, historical events, and technical terminology are essential to manuscript editors; keep the applicable style manual at hand if a different system of documentation is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chicago recommends Webster's Third New International and Merriam-Webster’s Collegiate; see bibliography for more reference works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping an editorial style sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an alphabetical style sheet for each manuscript listing words/terms to be capitalized, italicized, hyphenated, spelled, or otherwise treated uniquely to ensure consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes made simply to conform to house style need not be noted as exceptions; for paper manuscripts, note the page number of first occurrence. Note special punctuation, diacritics, and other items. Share the style sheet with author and publisher as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking limits and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are finally responsible for accuracy; most book publishers do not perform systematic fact-checking. Editors should point out obvious errors (including calculations) and query questionable names/references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be systematic about what to fact-check to avoid distraction; it may be efficient to correct obvious factual errors that can be easily double-checked, but anything beyond that should be limited to what is needed to form an effective query to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing front matter and titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Check half title, title page, table of contents, and list of illustrations against text and captions and applicable documentation; query discrepancies. Ensure order of elements and labeling for correct pagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may review author biographical notes and other front-matter elements though publishers usually prepare the copyright page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing chapter and part titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure part/chapter/article titles and subtitles are consistent with the text in spelling, hyphenation, and italics; recommend headline style for titles unless series/journal follows another capitalization style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check titles against table of contents and identify each title per the publisher’s manuscript requirements for electronic/paper manuscripts. Query discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing subheads
rubrics_metrics.description: Check subheads for consistency with text in spelling, hyphenation, italics, parallel structure, and tone; ensure hierarchy of subhead levels makes sense and is clearly identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If more than three levels of subhead, determine whether the lowest level can be eliminated. For electronic manuscripts, consider applying markup to preserve typographic distinctions. If subheads appear in the table of contents, cross-check for consistency. Chicago recommends headline style for subheads unless author has consistently used sentence style; if majority are sentences, sentence style may be preferred; no period added except for run-in heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing cross-references
rubrics_metrics.description: Check all references to tables, figures, appendixes, bibliographies, or other parts of a work for accuracy; point out and query discrepancies such as mismatched statistics or out-of-date table coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place-names on maps must match text spelling. Minimize or eliminate cross-references to specific pages. See also general cross-checking guidance (2.35).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing quotations and previously published material
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not alter quoted material except for light editing when translating or modernizing; transcribed interviews/field notes may be lightly edited; query misspellings and apparent transcription errors; ensure sources are given for quoted material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In editing previously published material, read for sense so nothing is out of order or inadvertently omitted; clarify ambiguous end-of-line hyphens in paper originals.
